b: The FY27 spending proposals include support for mass timber housing demonstrations, building code modernisation and the use of domestically produced wood products in federal buildings.
Mass timber is being promoted as a construction option to accelerate housing development and support domestic wood manufacturing in the US (Image: Unsplash)

The US Senate Appropriations Committee has included $20m in dedicated funding for mass timber initiatives in its Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27) spending proposals, alongside provisions supporting the use of innovative wood products in federal buildings.

The allocations are outlined in the explanatory statement accompanying the Senate’s Transportation, Housing and Urban Development (THUD) appropriations bill. A separate statement for the Financial Services and General Government (FSGG) bill supports the use of domestically produced bio-based materials, including mass timber, in federal construction.

Under the THUD proposal, $15m would be allocated to the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to develop, implement and evaluate a demonstration programme aimed at increasing the use of mass timber in housing.

The initiative would provide incentives of up to $20,000 per housing unit, with priority given to timber-rich regions where adoption remains low and markets close to mass timber suppliers. Up to $1m would also be used to develop educational resources for builders, developers, architects, structural engineers and other industry professionals.

A further $5m would be set aside under the PRO Housing programme for grants to help states and local authorities modernise building codes to incorporate mass timber provisions. These grants would also support faster project reviews, training and workforce development, as well as streamlined permitting for mass timber fabrication facilities.

The THUD explanatory statement cites research indicating that mass timber can reduce construction times by 15–25% compared with conventional building methods, potentially lowering overall project costs and allowing housing to be occupied sooner. It also identifies perceptions of higher costs as a barrier that the demonstration programme is intended to address.

The proposal includes an additional $3.3bn for the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) formula programme and $1.4bn for Economic Development Initiative projects. CDBG provides states and local authorities with funding to support housing rehabilitation and infrastructure development.

Mass timber construction has been recognised in the International Building Code since its 2021 edition, with the 2024 edition expanding on the provisions. However, differences in state and local building codes can still necessitate project-specific approvals, adding time and uncertainty to developments.

The American Wood Council (AWC) welcomed the proposed allocations. “Communities across the country need more housing, and they need it faster. Mass timber can help deliver it,” said AWC president and CEO Jackson Morrill. He added that greater demand for mass timber could support domestic manufacturing, from lumber mills to panel fabrication facilities, while creating jobs.

“Mass timber went through years of testing and rigorous review to earn its place in the model codes. This funding helps states and localities put those provisions to work, so builders can choose mass timber with confidence and without unnecessary delay,” said AWC vice-president of codes and regulations Phil Line.
